name: Zygomatic reduction

lead: Zygomatic reduction, also called malarplasty or cheekbone shaving, reshapes or repositions the cheekbones to give a narrower or flatter midface. People with a wide or prominent midface seek it for a slimmer facial width.

The cheek bone is cut and reshaped or moved inward, as forum posters describe it; some say shaving mainly reduces forward projection rather than width. On looksmax.org users debate whether width comes from bone or fat and whether the surgery improves proportions. The wiki's sources contain no outcome studies.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done under anaesthesia by a facial or plastic surgeon, popular in Asian aesthetic surgery. Swelling settles over weeks, and the final shape is judged after healing.
It is a bone-cutting operation under anaesthesia. Forum members report results ranging from very good to very bad, and no complication data were available in the sources used here.

angle.text: People with a wide or prominent midface want a narrower, slimmer facial width. The cheekbone is shaved or repositioned inward, so the change is visible after healing. Forum members report mixed before-and-after outcomes.

lead: Zygomatic reduction, also called reduction malarplasty, cheekbone reduction or cheekbone shaving, is surgery that narrows the cheekbones or lowers their projection, giving a slimmer, more oval facial outline.[1][2] People pursue it to reduce a wide midface, soften prominent cheek angles and balance the face against the jaw and forehead.[3] Because the zygomatic bones set the width of the face at cheek level, changing them changes the face's overall shape from the front.[4]

The operation is most associated with East Asia, where an oval or 'melon seed' face is considered delicate and attractive and cosmetic bone contouring has become increasingly popular; requests have also been rising in the United States.[1][3] One surgeon's report describes reduction malarplasty as the most common facial-contouring operation in Asian countries and says prominent zygomas are perceived by many Asian patients as unattractive.[5] The standard modern technique is an L-shaped osteotomy in which the zygomatic body and arch are cut, repositioned inward and fixed with screws, usually through incisions inside the mouth and a small incision by the sideburn.[6]

Published work is mainly surgical technique series and reviews. A 2023 meta-analysis pooled 29 studies and 6,611 patients to compare complications among reduction malarplasty methods.[7] In looksmaxxing forums the procedure is discussed in relation to face width, the eye-spacing ratio (ESR) and facial harmony, with before-and-after examples cited on both sides.[8][9][10]

paras: The zygomatic bone forms the cheekbone and part of the lateral and inferior wall of the eye socket; its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch, and the masseter muscle attaches to its lower border.[4] A review of skeletal contouring in ethnic patients states that the zygomaticomaxillary complex and mandible shape how overlying soft tissue is draped and lit, that their size and projection are sexually dimorphic and ethnically defined, and that excessive projection in any dimension can look undesirable to some patients.[3]

Aesthetic ideals vary: a cosmetic bone contouring review notes that in some cultures a wide jaw and square face are considered less attractive while an oval face is viewed as feminine and delicate.[1] Wikipedia notes that, in other cultures, high cheekbones are considered attractive and cheek augmentation is a cosmetic option, so the same bone can be a target for reduction or augmentation depending on the ideal.[4]

Surgeons distinguish a prominent zygomatic body (cheek projection) from a wide arch (width). The 2023 meta-analysis states that the L-shaped osteotomy gives a better effect when both body and arch protrude.[7] Reviews list reduction malarplasty together with mandibular angle and lateral cortex reduction and genioplasty as a family of facial skeleton procedures.[1]

Reduction malarplasty has been described in the plastic surgery literature since at least the early 1990s in the sources listed here, and a 2015 technical report cites a 1983 report as an earlier description.[11][12][5] Its author, a Seoul practitioner, cites later contributions including an intraoral approach from 2000 and a 2009 retrospective series of 418 cases using an intraoral L-shaped osteotomy.[5]

One L-shaped osteotomy technique through intraoral and sideburn incisions removes a middle segment of the anterior zygomatic body, fractures the arch root through a small incision, and repositions the freed complex medially with one or two screws; a series of 32 patients reported simple manipulation, stable fixation and less risk of a drooping face.[6] Another published variant, the rotation technique, removes no bone and instead rotates the most prominent point of the zygomaticomaxillary complex medially, contouring the posterior maxillary sinus wall to close the gap and fixing the segment with plates and screws; it is reported with photographs of two patients.[5]

Newer work describes digital planning, augmented reality and robot-assisted techniques in facial bone contouring, and an intraoral skeletal contouring simulator for surgeon training; the authors of the 2023 review say digital planning can shorten operative time and reduce bleeding.[13][14] A three-dimensional CT study of 80 patients after L-shaped malarplasty found that bone setback or resection correlated with changes in anterior and middle zygomatic width and protrusion, and the authors proposed a regression equation to help preoperative planning.[15]

The 2023 meta-analysis found that L-shaped osteotomy without bony resection had the lowest postoperative complication incidence (0.02%) but limits how much bone can be removed; with larger resections, long-arm and short-arm resection variants were each preferable depending on whether structural or functional complications were weighed.[7] A correction to the paper was later published.[16]

The Seoul surgeon's report names nonunion or malunion and drooping of the cheek as the two most common complications, and links nonunion to the masseter's attachment to the zygoma, arguing for rigid fixation and close bone contact.[5][4] Case reports describe maxillary sinusitis after the operation, including two cases treated with endoscopic sinus surgery.[17]

Because blood supply to the maxillofacial area is abundant and the intraoral field is narrow, hemostasis is a recognised challenge in facial contouring surgery; a randomized study of 282 patients across four contouring procedures evaluated a soluble hemostatic gauze.[18] Reviews advise that surgeons offering contouring operations be familiar with their potential complications.[1]

On looksmax.org the topic is raised mainly by people with wide faces. A poster asks whether cheekbone shaving could improve a ratio of 0.43 by narrowing the face and whether his zygomas are too narrow to qualify; replies include that the ratio is 'overrated' and that brow position matters more for harmony.[9] Another thread asks whether cheekbone shaving can fix a low ESR, with one poster arguing that shaving does little and that cutting a segment of the zygomatic arch and rejoining the ends is what reduces width; another reply suggests a longer face vertically is what is needed.[10]

A longer thread discusses wide skulls and 'bloated' faces, distinguishing fat from bone as the cause of width. The poster says buccal fat removal is often a poor decision because it can lead to an aged look, and says a slimmer face is generally better, citing malarplasty, 'shaving' and reduction as one and the same operation; another remark in the thread says shaving reduces forward projection more than width.[8] The thread contrasts an example described as very good with a public figure said to have lost his strengths after cheekbone and mandible work, and a reply says surgery should follow genuine need and warns of 'not knowing your face'.[8]
A further thread, titled around a 'ZSO malarplasty', asks whether the poster needs the procedure.[19]

Surgical reviews present reduction malarplasty and mandibuloplasty as techniques that can reshape the facial skeleton toward a desired shape, within the cultural framing of the patient's ideal.[3] The cosmetic bone contouring review states that these procedures 'may be performed to alter the facial contour and bring about dramatic results', and that surgeons should know the potential complications.[1]
No study found compares looksmaxxing-style ratios, such as ESR, before and after cheekbone surgery, and no randomized trial comparing surgery with no surgery on appearance was identified.

Evidence consists of surgical technique reports, reviews and observational series. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 studies (6,611 patients, literature from 1983 to early 2022) compared complications across reduction malarplasty methods.[7] A retrospective 3D CT study of 80 patients measured zygomatic width and protrusion changes after L-shaped malarplasty.[15] A 32-patient technique series reported outcomes of one L-shaped osteotomy approach.[6] A randomized study of 282 patients examined a hemostatic gauze across four facial contouring procedures,[18] and a randomized study evaluated a surgical training simulator for intraoral contouring operations.[14] No randomized trial comparing surgery with no surgery on appearance was identified.

lore.intro: Forum members discuss cheekbone shaving mainly for wide faces and as a way to change facial ratios, and they trade before-and-after examples.[8][9]

claims.claim: Cheekbone shaving mainly reduces forward projection, not width.
It can ascend a wide face but can harm a well-proportioned one.
Cheekbone surgery can raise the eye-to-eye spacing ratio (ESR).
A wide face may be bone or fat, and the cause matters for the choice of procedure.
The arch cut and reposition technique narrows the face with low complication rates.
Cheekbone reduction in Korea or other Asian centres is the destination for this surgery.
